title: Relationships
subtitle: flatmates, exes, getting on and falling out
summary: Name the people in your life - friends, mates, colleagues, partners and in-laws - and talk about liking, disliking, dating and falling out.

lesson.heading: Types of relationship
lesson.text: English has a fine scale of closeness: a **best friend** is closer than a **good friend**, who is closer than a **casual acquaintance** - someone you have met but don't know well.

examples.text: She's a **good friend** - she's not my **best friend**.
But she's more than just a **casual acquaintance**, right?
She wasn't in a **steady relationship** with anyone at the time.
examples.note: steady = fixed and not changing suddenly

examples.text: Kallum's living with his **parents-in-law** at the moment.

lesson.heading: -mate words and other labels
rows: someone in the same class as you
someone you share a room with
someone you share a flat or house with
someone you work with (informal, non-professional contexts)
someone you work with (professional, more formal)
a former partner (ex on its own is informal)
someone you live with but are not married to, or a business co-owner

lesson.heading: Internet relationships
lesson.text: If you join a social network, you **acquire friends** and build up your list of **contacts**. You can **invite** people to become your friends and **accept** new friends who invite you.

examples.text: You can **interact** with your friends by exchanging messages or **posting comments** on their page.
You can **share** photos and **tag** your friends in them.
examples.note: tag = name them in a photo you post

examples.text: If you want to finish a relationship, you can **unfriend** (or **defriend**) that person.

lesson.heading: Liking and not liking someone
lesson.note: She doesn't just like Ben, she idolises him. I really fancy Charlotte, but her friend just leaves me cold.

lesson.heading: Phrases and idioms for relationships and dating
rows: have a sexual relationship, usually secret
be friends again after a row
be seeing each other / date someone

lesson.text: People **make friends** - not ~~get friends~~ or ~~find friends~~. *It's often difficult to make new friends when you move to another city.*

exercises.prompt: This is Jack. He and I share a flat - we're ___.
exercises.explanation: Flatmate = a person you share a flat with.

exercises.prompt: Mike was the person I shared a room with at university - he was my ___.
exercises.explanation: Roommate = a person you share a room with.

exercises.prompt: We were in the same class together in 2006 - we were ___, weren't we?
exercises.explanation: Classmate = a person in the same class as you.

exercises.prompt: She's not really a friend; she's just someone I work with. In an informal, non-professional context you would call her a ___.
exercises.explanation: Workmate is informal; colleague is the more formal, professional word.

exercises.prompt: Sam has ___ you in a really funny photo on the social network.
exercises.explanation: To tag someone = to name them in a photo you post.

exercises.prompt: My grandma has just ___ me to be her friend online! I don't know if I should accept or not.
exercises.explanation: You invite people to become your friends, and you accept the invitations you want.

exercises.prompt: I'm going to ___ Emma if she keeps posting nasty comments about me online.
exercises.explanation: To unfriend or defriend someone is to remove them from your list of friends.

exercises.prompt: Match each idiom with its meaning.

pairs.right: be friends again after a row

exercises.statement: *Rosie and Matt don't get on eye to eye.*
exercises.explanation: The idiom is see eye to eye: Rosie and Matt don't see eye to eye.

exercises.statement: *We had a quarrel but now we've made it up.*
exercises.explanation: To make it up = to be friends again after a row.

exercises.statement: *Do you think Josh and Nuala are making an affair?*
exercises.explanation: You have an affair, not make one: Do you think Josh and Nuala are having an affair?

exercises.statement: *Maria seems to find it difficult to get friends among her classmates.*
exercises.explanation: People make friends: Maria seems to find it difficult to make friends among her classmates.

exercises.prompt: Does each verb express liking or disliking someone?

exercises.answer: I met my boyfriend at a party and we got together soon after.
exercises.explanation: To get together = to start a romantic relationship.
